doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Racial attitudes: growing up without prejudice and touring with a Black rhythm section
summary: He recalls no prejudice in England, and travelling in the 1950s with Wray Downes, Archie Alleyne and Bill Britto, staying in Black hotels.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What was the racial attitude like in Canada? Was it any different toward African- American musicians, or was it good, bad or indifferent?
I guess I’m thinking of when you first got there, or maybe in the 60s especially.

Fortunately for me I grew up in a small English town, and there was no prejudice. The first black person I saw was a soldier that my father took in during the war. I revered them because of my knowledge of Teddy Wilson and Lionel Hampton and Charlie Christian, Louis Armstrong. The man that inspired me to play jazz first of all was Coleman Hawkins. And to me they were gods basically. I didn’t know anything about prejudice. But there was a theory in New York at that time, in the 60s, that — I didn’t live there per se, so I didn’t experience it — but there was some kind of prejudice. Did they call it Uncle Tomism or something or other, or Tom Uncle?
Uncle Tom is a term, are you talking about prejudice against white jazz musicians?
Yeah. That you weren’t authentic. That what you played couldn’t be as good as a black musician.
Yeah, there was some of that, historically I guess.

Yeah. I never experienced it. I’ve always had wonderful reception and encouragement from musicians. I traveled with an all-black rhythm section in the 50s, from Canada. A wonderful pianist called Wray Downes; Archie Alleyne, a drummer; and Bill Britto, a bass player. I used to stay in black hotels in Detroit and Chicago, to be with them. I didn’t want to be apart and make them feel uncomfortable. But it was prejudiced, there was definite prejudice in those days. It wasn’t easy for any of the black people, was it?
